## Cited in this course

The learning-design advice in this course rests on a small number of well-known
sources: planning from the outcome backwards [@wiggins2005understanding],
writing objectives with concrete verbs [@anderson2001taxonomy], limiting how much
is new at once [@sweller1988cognitive], combining words with pictures
[@mayer2009multimedia], and using questions to help learners remember
[@roediger2006test]. The accessibility habits follow the Web Content
Accessibility Guidelines [@w3c2023wcag22].

::: {#refs}
:::

## Documentation of the tools

- **Quarto**, the program that builds the website: [quarto.org/docs/guide](https://quarto.org/docs/guide/).
  The section on *Websites* and the one on *Visual Editor* are the most useful.
- **GitHub Pages**: [docs.github.com/pages](https://docs.github.com/pages).
- **GitLab Pages**: [docs.gitlab.com/user/project/pages](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/project/pages/).

## Suggested next steps

- Read one of the sources above in full. The book on *Understanding by Design*
  changes how many people plan every course afterwards.
- Take one chapter of an existing lecture of yours and turn it into a chapter of
  a course, using the skeleton in `_chapter-skeleton.qmd`.
- Ask a colleague to review your first chapter using the checklist in
  Chapter 7.
